newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Land claim decision hailed by Wik lawyer.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Land claim decision hailed by Wik lawyer.

text.p: Australia's High Court ruled on Monday that the granting of a pastoral lease did not necessarily wipe out any Aboriginal land claims on the same area.

Australia's highest court of appeal found that the claim of an Aboriginal group, the Wik people, over 35,000 square km of land in far-north Queensland may extinguish the rights of the 12 pastoral leaseholders in that area.
The judgment was split four-to-three in favour of the Wik people's claim.
The group was appealing an earlier judgment in Australia's Federal Court, which found that pastoral leases took precedence over Aboriginal land claims.
Lawyer James Fitzgerald, representing the Wik people, told reporters the decision was a win for both Aborigines and pastoralists.
He said the decision was in favour of co-existence.

"The High Court has made it clear that wherever the rights of pastoralists are in conflict with the exercise of native title rights that the rights of pastoralists will prevail," Fitzgerald told reporters outside the court.
"As a result, there is no loser from today's decision."
He said the decision specifically targeted the land claims in Cape York in northern Queensland state, but it may have far-reaching implications.
"The High Court's decision technically appplies only to the western Cape York peninsula, but it will certainly have implications elsewhere in Australia," he said.

Lawyer Mark Love, who repesented the Cattlemen's Union, said the decision would increase uncertainty for pastoral leaseholders because it meant they had to work out exactly what rights they hold in regard to their land.
"Obviously, we're disappointed with the outcome of the case (because) it hasn't delivered the degree of certainty that we had hoped for," Love told reporters.
Love said it was too early to determine what implications the decision had for the rest of Australia.
"We would hope to be able to pull from the judgments some guidance as to how native title will pursue and how other land tenures can stand consistently with that," he said.
The case will now go back to the Federal Court where the Wik people will have to prove their right to the land.
